edges.description: The genetic predisposition manifests as transient hyperexcitability of the maturing perirolandic cortex.

In a minority of children the same inherited seizure susceptibility is expressed earlier as febrile seizures, before the centrotemporal-spike epilepsy declares itself; febrile seizures are an antecedent of the syndrome rather than a consequence of its discharges.
The hyperexcitable perirolandic cortex generates centrotemporal spikes, strongly activated by sleep.
The discharges manifest clinically as focal perirolandic seizures.
Frequent epileptiform activity, especially in sleep, transiently disrupts language and cognitive networks.
The high-amplitude, sleep-activated centrotemporal spike-waves recorded on EEG are the direct scalp expression of these discharges.
The perirolandic seizure is a focal-onset seizure, characteristically nocturnal and arising in mid-childhood.
Onset in the perirolandic somatosensory cortex produces the unilateral perioral or intraoral paresthesia that commonly opens the seizure.
Involvement of the oropharyngeal motor strip produces speech arrest and anarthria/dysarthria during the seizure.
The same oropharyngeal perirolandic involvement produces the near-defining ictal hypersalivation and drooling.
A focal perirolandic seizure may propagate bilaterally and evolve into a bilateral tonic-clonic seizure.

The dysfunction presents clinically as specific language and learning difficulties during the active epilepsy period. Whether it fully resolves with seizure remission is not settled - deficits have been found to persist in children already in remission.

nodes.description: During a maturational window in mid-childhood, the perirolandic (centrotemporal) sensorimotor cortex becomes transiently hyperexcitable; the age-restricted nature of this hyperexcitability underlies both the childhood onset and the spontaneous remission with brain maturation. This node captures the single concept of the maturation-dependent cortical hyperexcitability.
